front: Which beta-blockers are beta-1 selective, and which also block alpha-1?
bottom: Metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol: beta-1 selective.

bullets.clue: Selectivity fades at high doses.
bullets.treat: Carvedilol and labetalol add alpha-1 blockade. HFrEF: only metoprolol succinate, carvedilol or bisoprolol.
bullets.trap: Pindolol and acebutolol have ISA: avoid after MI and in HFrEF.

back: Metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol: beta-1 selective. Key clue: Selectivity fades at high doses. Pharmacist move: Carvedilol and labetalol add alpha-1 blockade. HFrEF: only metoprolol succinate, carvedilol or bisoprolol. Exam trap: Pindolol and acebutolol have ISA: avoid after MI and in HFrEF.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol: beta-1 selective.

source.recommendation: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF: in HFrEF use one of the three evidence-based beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, sustained-release metoprolol succinate) (COR 1). Selectivity and alpha/ISA properties per FDA labeling.

topic: Anticholinergic burden: mechanism & classic adverse effects
front: An 80-year-old on diphenhydramine and oxybutynin is newly confused. What's the mechanism, and what does Beers say?
bottom: Anticholinergic burden: avoid in older adults.

bullets.clue: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, delirium.
bullets.treat: Stop or swap strongly anticholinergic drugs: diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, oxybutynin, amitriptyline, paroxetine.
bullets.trap: Burden is cumulative: minimize combined anticholinergics, not just one drug.

back: Anticholinergic burden: avoid in older adults. Key clue: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, delirium. Pharmacist move: Stop or swap strongly anticholinergic drugs: diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, oxybutynin, amitriptyline, paroxetine. Exam trap: Burden is cumulative: minimize combined anticholinergics, not just one drug.
mnemonic: Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't poop.

diagram.alt: Text card. Anticholinergic burden: avoid in older adults.

source.recommendation: AGS Beers Criteria 2023: avoid strongly anticholinergic drugs in older adults (delirium, falls, constipation, urinary retention); minimize the number of anticholinergic drugs used together.

topic: Serotonin syndrome vs NMS mechanisms and culprit drugs
front: New tramadol on top of sertraline; next day clonus, hyperreflexia, fever. Serotonin syndrome or NMS?

bullets.clue: Hunter criteria: spontaneous, inducible or ocular clonus with a serotonergic drug.
bullets.treat: Stop serotonergic drugs; supportive care, benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine if needed.
bullets.trap: NMS: antipsychotic, days of onset, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia.

back: Serotonin syndrome: fast onset, clonus. Key clue: Hunter criteria: spontaneous, inducible or ocular clonus with a serotonergic drug. Pharmacist move: Stop serotonergic drugs; supportive care, benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine if needed. Exam trap: NMS: antipsychotic, days of onset, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia.

diagram.alt: Steps. Serotonin syndrome: fast onset, clonus.

source.recommendation: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria (QJM 2003): serotonergic agent plus spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor plus hyperreflexia; or hypertonia, temperature >38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus. Management per labeling of serotonergic drugs.

topic: QT-prolonging drug classes and additive risk
front: Which common drugs stack QT risk, and what do you check before combining them?
bottom: Additive QT drugs raise torsades risk.

bullets.clue: Macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron, methadone, citalopram, haloperidol, sotalol, dofetilide, amiodarone.
bullets.treat: Baseline ECG; correct potassium and magnesium; choose a non-QT alternative.
bullets.trap: Citalopram: max 20 mg/day over age 60.

back: Additive QT drugs raise torsades risk. Key clue: Macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron, methadone, citalopram, haloperidol, sotalol, dofetilide, amiodarone. Pharmacist move: Baseline ECG; correct potassium and magnesium; choose a non-QT alternative. Exam trap: Citalopram: max 20 mg/day over age 60.

diagram.alt: Steps. Additive QT drugs raise torsades risk.

source.recommendation: CredibleMeds QTdrugs list (known TdP risk includes azithromycin, clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ondansetron, methadone, citalopram, haloperidol, sotalol, dofetilide, amiodarone). Citalopram labeling: 20 mg/day max in patients >60 years; correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia.

topic: CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers (clarithro, azoles, ritonavir, rifampin, carbamazepine)
front: A patient on simvastatin is prescribed clarithromycin. What's the problem, and who else does this?
bottom: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor: statin levels spike.

bullets.clue: Inhibitors: clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, grapefruit juice. Inducers: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort.
bullets.treat: Simvastatin or lovastatin plus strong 3A4 inhibitor: contraindicated; hold statin or switch antibiotic.
bullets.trap: Azithromycin is not a meaningful 3A4 inhibitor.

back: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor: statin levels spike. Key clue: Inhibitors: clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, grapefruit juice. Inducers: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort. Pharmacist move: Simvastatin or lovastatin plus strong 3A4 inhibitor: contraindicated; hold statin or switch antibiotic. Exam trap: Azithromycin is not a meaningful 3A4 inhibitor.

diagram.alt: Steps. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor: statin levels spike.

source.guideline: ICH M12 Drug Interaction guidance 2024 (supersedes FDA 2020 DDI guidances); FDA labeling
source.recommendation: ICH M12 Drug Interaction Studies (FDA final 2024) frames index inhibitors/inducers. Simvastatin and lovastatin labeling: contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (itraconazole, ketoconazole, clarithromycin, HIV protease inhibitors, cobicistat).

front: Why do two patients need very different warfarin doses for the same INR goal?
bottom: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 variants lower dose needs.

bullets.clue: CYP2C9 *2/*3 slow S-warfarin clearance; VKORC1 variant raises sensitivity.
bullets.treat: CPIC: use a validated genotype-guided algorithm; start lower in variant carriers.
bullets.trap: Genotype changes the dose, not the INR target.

back: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 variants lower dose needs. Key clue: CYP2C9 *2/*3 slow S-warfarin clearance; VKORC1 variant raises sensitivity. Pharmacist move: CPIC: use a validated genotype-guided algorithm; start lower in variant carriers. Exam trap: Genotype changes the dose, not the INR target.

diagram.alt: Steps. CYP2C9 and VKORC1 variants lower dose needs.

source.recommendation: CPIC 2017 warfarin guideline: use a validated pharmacogenetic algorithm incorporating CYP2C9 and VKORC1 (and CYP4F2 where applicable) to calculate the dose; decreased-function CYP2C9 alleles and VKORC1 -1639A require lower doses.

front: Post-PCI patient is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. Is clopidogrel right?
bottom: No: clopidogrel won't activate. Use prasugrel or ticagrelor.

bullets.clue: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19; *2/*3 are loss-of-function.
bullets.treat: CPIC 2022 for ACS/PCI: poor or intermediate metabolizers get prasugrel or ticagrelor if no contraindication.
bullets.trap: Clopidogrel's boxed warning (2010): diminished effect in poor metabolizers.

back: No: clopidogrel won't activate. Use prasugrel or ticagrelor. Key clue: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19; *2/*3 are loss-of-function. Pharmacist move: CPIC 2022 for ACS/PCI: poor or intermediate metabolizers get prasugrel or ticagrelor if no contraindication. Exam trap: Clopidogrel's boxed warning (2010): diminished effect in poor metabolizers.

diagram.alt: Text card. No: clopidogrel won't activate. Use prasugrel or ticagrelor.

source.recommendation: CPIC 2022: CYP2C19 poor and intermediate metabolizers with ACS/PCI: avoid standard-dose clopidogrel; use prasugrel or ticagrelor if no contraindication. FDA boxed warning: diminished antiplatelet effect in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers.

front: Which HLA tests come before carbamazepine and allopurinol, and why?
bottom: HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine; HLA-B*58:01 for allopurinol.

bullets.clue: Both alleles predict SJS/TEN (allopurinol: also DRESS).
bullets.treat: Positive: avoid the drug and choose an alternative (febuxostat for gout).
bullets.trap: ACR 2020: test HLA-B*58:01 before allopurinol in Southeast Asian and African American patients.

back: HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine; HLA-B*58:01 for allopurinol. Key clue: Both alleles predict SJS/TEN (allopurinol: also DRESS). Pharmacist move: Positive: avoid the drug and choose an alternative (febuxostat for gout). Exam trap: ACR 2020: test HLA-B*58:01 before allopurinol in Southeast Asian and African American patients.

diagram.alt: Text card. HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine; HLA-B*58:01 for allopurinol.

source.recommendation: CPIC 2017: HLA-B*15:02 positive, carbamazepine-naive: do not use carbamazepine (oxcarbazepine likewise). CPIC 2015: HLA-B*58:01 positive: allopurinol contraindicated. ACR 2020 gout: conditionally recommends HLA-B*58:01 testing before allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian descent and African American patients.

topic: TPMT/NUDT15 and thiopurines; DPYD and fluoropyrimidines
front: Before azathioprine or capecitabine, which genes matter, and what happens with low activity?
bottom: TPMT/NUDT15 for thiopurines; DPYD for fluoropyrimidines.

bullets.clue: Low enzyme activity causes life-threatening myelosuppression or toxicity.
bullets.treat: Thiopurine poor metabolizer: drastic dose cut or alternative. DPYD poor metabolizer: avoid 5-FU and capecitabine.
bullets.trap: DPYD intermediate metabolizer: start at 50% dose.

back: TPMT/NUDT15 for thiopurines; DPYD for fluoropyrimidines. Key clue: Low enzyme activity causes life-threatening myelosuppression or toxicity. Pharmacist move: Thiopurine poor metabolizer: drastic dose cut or alternative. DPYD poor metabolizer: avoid 5-FU and capecitabine. Exam trap: DPYD intermediate metabolizer: start at 50% dose.

diagram.alt: Text card. TPMT/NUDT15 for thiopurines; DPYD for fluoropyrimidines.

source.recommendation: CPIC TPMT/NUDT15 2025 update: poor metabolizers—malignancy: markedly reduced thiopurine dose with less frequent dosing; nonmalignant conditions: consider alternative; intermediate: reduced starting dose. CPIC DPYD (2024 update): activity score 0 or poor metabolizer—avoid fluoropyrimidines; intermediate (activity 1 or 1.5)—reduce starting dose by 50%.

front: Phenytoin level is 8 on 300 mg/day. Why not just jump to 400 mg?

bullets.clue: Near Vmax, metabolism saturates; small dose increases cause big level jumps.
bullets.treat: Increase in small steps (30–100 mg/day) and recheck after steady state.
bullets.trap: Total range 10–20 mcg/mL; use free level (1–2) in low albumin or renal failure.

back: Michaelis-Menten: levels rise disproportionately. Key clue: Near Vmax, metabolism saturates; small dose increases cause big level jumps. Pharmacist move: Increase in small steps (30–100 mg/day) and recheck after steady state. Exam trap: Total range 10–20 mcg/mL; use free level (1–2) in low albumin or renal failure.

diagram.alt: Phenytoin Michaelis-Menten curve: steady-state level rises disproportionately as dose nears Vmax. Illustrative patient (Km 4 mg/L, Vmax 450 mg/day): 300 mg/day gives 8, 350 gives 14, 400 gives 32 mcg/mL.

source.recommendation: Phenytoin labeling: nonlinear (saturable) kinetics; small dose increments can cause large serum concentration increases; total therapeutic 10–20 mcg/mL, unbound 1–2 mcg/mL. Applied clinical PK (Winter's Basic Clinical Pharmacokinetics): Michaelis-Menten dosing.

topic: Bioavailability, salt factor and bioequivalence (AB rating)
front: Two generics are both 'AB' in the Orange Book. What does that mean, and how is bioequivalence shown?

bullets.clue: 90% CI for AUC and Cmax ratios within 80–125%.
bullets.treat: Substitute AB-rated products. Route or salt change: dose × F (bioavailability) × S (salt fraction).
bullets.trap: B codes (e.g., BX) are not considered equivalent: don't substitute.

back: AB = therapeutically equivalent; substitutable. Key clue: 90% CI for AUC and Cmax ratios within 80–125%. Pharmacist move: Substitute AB-rated products. Route or salt change: dose × F (bioavailability) × S (salt fraction). Exam trap: B codes (e.g., BX) are not considered equivalent: don't substitute.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. AB = therapeutically equivalent; substitutable.

source.recommendation: FDA Orange Book preface: 'A' codes = therapeutically equivalent; AB = actual or potential bioequivalence problems resolved with adequate evidence; 'B' codes = not considered therapeutically equivalent. Bioequivalence: 90% CIs for AUC and Cmax geometric mean ratios within 80–125%.

topic: Study design, bias, and choosing the statistical test (t-test, chi-square, ANOVA)
front: Comparing mean A1c across three drug groups. Which test, and what if it's yes/no data?

bullets.clue: Two independent means: t-test; paired before/after: paired t-test.
bullets.treat: Nominal outcomes: chi-square; ordinal or skewed: Mann-Whitney (2) or Kruskal-Wallis (3+).
bullets.trap: Don't run repeated t-tests across 3+ groups: it inflates type I error.

back: Three-plus group means: ANOVA. Key clue: Two independent means: t-test; paired before/after: paired t-test. Pharmacist move: Nominal outcomes: chi-square; ordinal or skewed: Mann-Whitney (2) or Kruskal-Wallis (3+). Exam trap: Don't run repeated t-tests across 3+ groups: it inflates type I error.

diagram.alt: Steps. Three-plus group means: ANOVA.

source.recommendation: CONSORT 2025 statement (30-item checklist) for trial reporting. Test selection per standard biostatistics references: ANOVA for 3+ group means (multiple t-tests inflate type I error); chi-square for nominal data; Mann-Whitney/Kruskal-Wallis for ordinal or non-normal data.

topic: Drug stability & storage (insulin, vaccines, nitroglycerin, dabigatran bottle)
front: Storage counseling: in-use insulin pen, nitroglycerin SL tablets, dabigatran capsules. What's the rule for each?
bottom: Store each one exactly as labeled.

bullets.clue: In-use insulin at room temp for a product-specific time (glargine 28 days, degludec 56).
bullets.treat: Nitroglycerin: original glass bottle, cap tight. Dabigatran: original bottle; use within 4 months of opening.
bullets.trap: Refrigerated vaccines: 2–8 °C; freezing ruins them.

back: Store each one exactly as labeled. Key clue: In-use insulin at room temp for a product-specific time (glargine 28 days, degludec 56). Pharmacist move: Nitroglycerin: original glass bottle, cap tight. Dabigatran: original bottle; use within 4 months of opening. Exam trap: Refrigerated vaccines: 2–8 °C; freezing ruins them.

diagram.alt: Steps. Store each one exactly as labeled.

source.guideline: USP <659>; FDA labeling; CDC Vaccine Storage & Handling Toolkit (updated Jul 2026)
source.recommendation: FDA labeling: insulin glargine in-use 28 days, insulin degludec 56 days at room temperature; nitroglycerin SL in original glass container; dabigatran in original bottle, discard 4 months after opening. CDC Vaccine Storage & Handling Toolkit: refrigerated vaccines 2–8 °C (36–46 °F), do not freeze. USP <659> defines storage terms.

topic: Nonsterile compounding: BUD defaults by preparation type
front: Nonsterile compounding without stability data: what are the default BUDs by preparation type?

bullets.clue: Aqueous unpreserved 14 days refrigerated; aqueous preserved 35 days.
bullets.treat: Nonaqueous 90 days; solid dosage forms 180 days.
bullets.trap: BUD can't exceed the earliest expiration of any ingredient.

back: Water drives the BUD. Key clue: Aqueous unpreserved 14 days refrigerated; aqueous preserved 35 days. Pharmacist move: Nonaqueous 90 days; solid dosage forms 180 days. Exam trap: BUD can't exceed the earliest expiration of any ingredient.

diagram.alt: Steps. Water drives the BUD.

source.recommendation: USP <795> (official Nov 1, 2023) default BUDs: aqueous, nonpreserved: 14 days refrigerated; aqueous, preserved: 35 days (CRT or refrigerated); nonaqueous: 90 days; solid: 180 days; BUD may not exceed the earliest expiration date of any component.

topic: Sterile compounding: Category 1/2/3 BUDs and ISO classes
front: Sterile compounding: what separates Category 1, 2 and 3 CSPs?
bottom: Category drives BUD and room requirements.

bullets.clue: Category 1: SCA allowed; BUD 12 h room temp or 24 h refrigerated.
bullets.treat: Category 2: cleanroom suite; aseptic, sterile ingredients, no sterility test: 4 days room temp, 10 refrigerated, 45 frozen.
bullets.trap: Category 3 needs sterility testing; immediate-use CSPs: 4 hours.

back: Category drives BUD and room requirements. Key clue: Category 1: SCA allowed; BUD 12 h room temp or 24 h refrigerated. Pharmacist move: Category 2: cleanroom suite; aseptic, sterile ingredients, no sterility test: 4 days room temp, 10 refrigerated, 45 frozen. Exam trap: Category 3 needs sterility testing; immediate-use CSPs: 4 hours.

diagram.alt: Steps. Category drives BUD and room requirements.

source.recommendation: USP <797> (official Nov 1, 2023): Category 1 BUD ≤12 h CRT or ≤24 h refrigerated, may be compounded in an SCA; Category 2 in cleanroom suite, default BUD for aseptically prepared CSP from sterile starting components without sterility testing: 4 days CRT, 10 days refrigerated, 45 days frozen; Category 3 requires sterility testing and additional requirements; immediate-use CSPs administered within 4 h. PEC = ISO Class 5; buffer room ISO 7; ante-room ISO 8 (ISO 7 if opening to negative-pressure room).

topic: Hazardous drug handling: C-PEC/C-SEC, PPE, NIOSH list
front: Compounding antineoplastic hazardous drugs: what room, what hood, what PPE?

bullets.clue: C-SEC externally vented, negative 0.01–0.03 inch water column.
bullets.treat: Two pairs ASTM D6978 chemo gloves and a hazardous-drug gown.
bullets.trap: Never compound HDs in a positive-pressure room; C-SEC at −0.01 to −0.03 in. water column.

back: C-PEC inside a negative-pressure C-SEC. Key clue: C-SEC externally vented, negative 0.01–0.03 inch water column. Pharmacist move: Two pairs ASTM D6978 chemo gloves and a hazardous-drug gown. Exam trap: Never compound HDs in a positive-pressure room; C-SEC at −0.01 to −0.03 in. water column.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. C-PEC inside a negative-pressure C-SEC.

source.recommendation: USP <800> (compendially applicable Nov 1, 2023): sterile and nonsterile HD compounding in a C-PEC within a C-SEC that is externally vented with negative pressure between 0.01 and 0.03 inches of water column; two pairs of chemotherapy gloves meeting ASTM D6978 and gowns shown to resist HD permeability for compounding. NIOSH List of Hazardous Drugs in Healthcare Settings, 2024.

topic: Levigation, geometric dilution, suppository displacement factor
front: Mixing 50 mg of a potent drug into 50 g of base, then making suppositories. Which techniques?

bullets.clue: Geometric dilution: mix drug with equal part diluent, keep doubling.
bullets.treat: Levigate with mineral oil (oleaginous) or glycerin (aqueous) to smooth particles.
bullets.trap: Base per suppository = blank weight − (drug weight ÷ density factor).

back: Geometric dilution; levigation; displacement factor. Key clue: Geometric dilution: mix drug with equal part diluent, keep doubling. Pharmacist move: Levigate with mineral oil (oleaginous) or glycerin (aqueous) to smooth particles. Exam trap: Base per suppository = blank weight − (drug weight ÷ density factor).

diagram.alt: Text card. Geometric dilution; levigation; displacement factor.

source.recommendation: USP <795> requires procedures ensuring uniform mixing; standard compounding references (Remington) describe geometric dilution, levigation with a compatible levigating agent, and displacement (density) factor calculation for suppositories.

front: Calc: 70-year-old man, 5'10", 80 kg, SCr 1.2 mg/dL. Cockcroft-Gault CrCl?

bullets.clue: IBW = 50 + 2.3 × 10 = 73 kg (actual is within 120%, use IBW).
bullets.trap: Women: multiply by 0.85. Obese (>120% IBW): use adjusted weight.

back: CrCl ≈ 59 mL/min. Given: IBW = 50 + 2.3 × 10 = 73 kg (actual is within 120%, use IBW). Work: (140 − 70) × 73 ÷ (72 × 1.2) = 5110 ÷ 86.4 = 59. Exam trap: Women: multiply by 0.85. Obese (>120% IBW): use adjusted weight.

diagram.alt: Threshold. CrCl ≈ 59 mL/min.

source.recommendation: Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. Nephron 1976: CrCl = (140 − age) × weight / (72 × SCr), × 0.85 for females. Weight choice (IBW; adjusted weight if >120% IBW) per common clinical practice. FDA 2024 renal guidance allows eGFR or CrCl for labeling.

front: Calc: woman, 5'4", 90 kg. IBW and adjusted body weight?

bullets.clue: Devine female: 45.5 + 2.3 kg per inch over 5 ft.
bullets.trap: Male base is 50 kg, not 45.5.

back: IBW 54.7 kg; AdjBW 68.8 kg. Given: Devine female: 45.5 + 2.3 kg per inch over 5 ft. Work: IBW = 45.5 + 2.3 × 4 = 54.7. AdjBW = 54.7 + 0.4 × (90 − 54.7) = 68.8. Exam trap: Male base is 50 kg, not 45.5.

diagram.alt: Text card. IBW 54.7 kg; AdjBW 68.8 kg.

source.recommendation: Devine 1974: IBW male = 50 kg + 2.3 kg/inch over 60 in; female = 45.5 kg + 2.3 kg/inch over 60 in. Adjusted body weight = IBW + 0.4 × (TBW − IBW).

front: Calc: 170 cm, 70 kg. Mosteller BSA, and the dose at 75 mg/m²?

bullets.clue: BSA = √(height cm × weight kg ÷ 3600).
bullets.trap: Square root of the whole product, not of each term.

back: BSA 1.82 m²; dose 136 mg. Given: BSA = √(height cm × weight kg ÷ 3600). Work: √(170 × 70 ÷ 3600) = √3.31 = 1.82; 1.82 × 75 = 136 mg. Exam trap: Square root of the whole product, not of each term.

diagram.alt: Threshold. BSA 1.82 m²; dose 136 mg.

source.recommendation: Mosteller RD. NEJM 1987: BSA (m²) = √(height cm × weight kg / 3600).

front: Calc: total calcium 7.6 mg/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL. Corrected calcium?

bullets.clue: Corrected Ca = measured + 0.8 × (4 − albumin).
bullets.trap: No calcium replacement for 'low' total Ca that corrects to normal; check ionized Ca if unsure.

back: Corrected Ca = 9.2 mg/dL: normal. Given: Corrected Ca = measured + 0.8 × (4 − albumin). Work: 7.6 + 0.8 × (4 − 2.0) = 7.6 + 1.6 = 9.2. Exam trap: No calcium replacement for 'low' total Ca that corrects to normal; check ionized Ca if unsure.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Corrected Ca = 9.2 mg/dL: normal.

source.recommendation: Payne RB et al. BMJ 1973 albumin adjustment; commonly applied as corrected Ca (mg/dL) = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL). Ionized calcium is preferred when accuracy matters.

front: Calc: Na 140, Cl 100, HCO3 12; measured osm 320; glucose 90, BUN 14. Anion gap and osmolal gap?
bottom: AG 28; osmolal gap 30: think toxic alcohol.

bullets.clue: AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3). Calculated osm = 2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8.
bullets.trap: Gap >10 plus high-AG acidosis: start fomepizole.

back: AG 28; osmolal gap 30: think toxic alcohol. Given: AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3). Calculated osm = 2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8. Work: AG = 140 − 112 = 28. Calc osm = 280 + 5 + 5 = 290; gap = 320 − 290 = 30. Exam trap: Gap >10 plus high-AG acidosis: start fomepizole.

diagram.alt: Steps. AG 28; osmolal gap 30: think toxic alcohol.

source.recommendation: Standard formulas: anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3), normal ~8–12; calculated serum osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; osmolal gap >10 suggests unmeasured osmoles (methanol, ethylene glycol). Fomepizole is the antidote for toxic alcohols per antidote references.

front: Calc: phenytoin 8 mcg/mL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, normal renal function. Corrected level?

bullets.clue: Sheiner-Tozer: measured ÷ (0.2 × albumin + 0.1).
bullets.trap: Don't increase the dose: it's in range. ESRD uses 0.1 × albumin.

back: Corrected phenytoin = 16 mcg/mL. Given: Sheiner-Tozer: measured ÷ (0.2 × albumin + 0.1). Work: 8 ÷ (0.2 × 2.0 + 0.1) = 8 ÷ 0.5 = 16. Exam trap: Don't increase the dose: it's in range. ESRD uses 0.1 × albumin.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Corrected phenytoin = 16 mcg/mL.

source.guideline: Sheiner-Tozer equation (Sheiner & Tozer 1978; review Ann Pharmacother 2016)
source.recommendation: Sheiner-Tozer: corrected phenytoin = measured / (0.2 × albumin + 0.1); in ESRD/severe renal impairment use (0.1 × albumin + 0.1). Therapeutic total 10–20 mcg/mL.

front: Calc: TC 200, HDL 50, TG 150 mg/dL. Friedewald LDL-C and non-HDL-C?

bullets.clue: LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5. Non-HDL = TC − HDL.
bullets.trap: 2026 guideline prefers Martin/Hopkins or Sampson/NIH over Friedewald; Friedewald fails at TG ≥400.

back: LDL-C 120; non-HDL-C 150. Given: LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5. Non-HDL = TC − HDL. Work: 200 − 50 − 30 = 120. Non-HDL = 200 − 50 = 150. Exam trap: 2026 guideline prefers Martin/Hopkins or Sampson/NIH over Friedewald; Friedewald fails at TG ≥400.

diagram.alt: Text card. LDL-C 120; non-HDL-C 150.

source.recommendation: Friedewald 1972 (Clin Chem): LDL-C = TC − HDL-C − TG/5 (mg/dL), not valid when TG ≥400 mg/dL. 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia guideline (COR 1): Martin/Hopkins or Sampson/NIH equation preferred over Friedewald to estimate LDL-C. Non-HDL-C = TC − HDL-C.

front: Calc: patient on clozapine, WBC 3,000/mm³, segs 40%, bands 5%. ANC, and what now?

bullets.clue: ANC = WBC × (% segs + % bands).
bullets.treat: 3,000 × 0.45 = 1,350. Continue; monitor ANC three times weekly until ≥1,500.
bullets.trap: REMS is gone since 2025; the label's ANC monitoring still applies.

back: ANC 1,350: mild neutropenia; continue clozapine. Given: ANC = WBC × (% segs + % bands). Work: 3,000 × 0.45 = 1,350. Continue; monitor ANC three times weekly until ≥1,500. Exam trap: REMS is gone since 2025; the label's ANC monitoring still applies.

diagram.alt: Steps. ANC 1,350: mild neutropenia; continue clozapine.

source.recommendation: Clozapine labeling (general population): ANC ≥1500 normal; mild neutropenia 1000–1499: continue treatment, ANC three times weekly until ≥1500; moderate 500–999: interrupt; severe <500: interrupt. FDA eliminated the clozapine REMS (2025); monitoring per labeling continues.
